findings.claim: The explore result looks spread over 11 spells, but it rests on a few market episodes. The 8-spell floor counts runs of the S&P below −5%, so fragments of one episode count separately, and the sealed read could clear the floor on only a few real episodes.
findings.evidence: Report § 'Are the stressed days spread over the tape?': stressed Elevated rows are 2010: 38 (3 spells), 2011: 72 (4 spells), 2014: 4 (1), 2015: 31 (2), 2016: 24 (1), and 0 in every other year. That puts 110 of 169 rows (65%) in 2010–2011 and 55 in 2015–16. Report § Gold structure check: 'spells = distinct runs of the S&P below −5% in the cell'. The spell counts overlap across cells (Elevated 11 + Normal 27 = 38, against 31 for the whole stressed bin in § 'stressed alone'), so one drawdown can be counted in both cells. The entry's floor (§2, What would test it): 'fewer than 150 rows or fewer than 8 distinct stress spells makes the read underpowered'. The floor is met as the entry defines it, which is why this finding is not blocking.

findings.claim: The entry rules out Gold's own volatility, but not S&P drawdown depth as a rival. The stressed bin joins the harness's −5% to −10% and ≤ −10% bins. Fragile days probably sit in the deeper drawdowns, where margin-call selling would also be stronger. A width split that survives dividing out volatility could then be a depth effect, and the read would credit it to the OR state.
findings.evidence: Entry §2, Explore-tier looks: 'DD_EDGES = (−5%, −10%)'. Entry §2, Mechanism: 'In a stressed S&P tape (drawdown ≤ −5%)'. Report § Gold structure check collapses the stressed side to 'dd<=-5' and offers only a 'stressed alone — the dose-response rival' table at the bin level. No Elevated-vs-Normal contrast within a single depth bin appears anywhere. §9 q5: 'Prefer the contrast that only the mechanism produces — within-episode, or against the rival dimension.' Not blocking, because the named confound does have a test and the rule says 'prefer'.

brief.case_against:
I found nothing that breaks the rules. The dates line up: the prediction was committed the day before the data run and was not changed afterwards. Every number matches the report. The data used is all from before the sealed period.

The strongest honest argument against promotion is this. The pattern in older data comes mostly from two market scares, 2010–2011 and 2015–16; about two-thirds of the fragile, stressed days fall in 2010–2011. The entry counts 11 'spells', but one choppy sell-off that keeps crossing the −5% line counts several times. The same counting could let the one-time sealed read pass its minimum-evidence rule on only three or four real events.

The entry also has not ruled out a simpler explanation: fragile days may just be days when stocks had fallen further. Deeper falls alone could make gold swing more.

Finally, the prior is low. The model's measured skill in older data is a small fraction of what the bar requires. The entry says so openly.
brief.what_it_claims: When US stocks have already fallen meaningfully and the market's fragility alarm is on, gold's outcomes over the next one to four weeks spread out more in both directions than on stressed days without the alarm. It claims the spread is wider than gold's own recent volatility would explain. It makes no claim about which way gold moves.
brief.what_would_change_it: My concerns would weaken if the entry counted distinct market episodes rather than runs across the −5% line, and set its minimum-evidence rule on those episodes. They would also weaken if a counted check showed the alarm still widens gold's spread among days with the same depth of stock decline. If the widening disappeared within a single depth band, the alarm would not be doing the work.

brief.case_against: The entry changed its own test after seeing the answer and then said it hadn't. Before the data was run, it predicted that Gold's typical range of outcomes would be at least 1.4 times wider on fragile, stressed days than on calm stressed days. The data came back at about 1.3 times at one week and just under 1.4 at two weeks, so the prediction failed. The next day the bar was lowered to 1.2, which the data passes. The entry then describes this as the pre-registered prediction holding, committed before the run. That is exactly the move the rules exist to stop. A secondary concern: most of the fragile stressed days come from 2010–2011, so the pattern may reflect one turbulent period for Gold. Finally, the entry itself admits the chance of passing the product bar on the sealed data is low.
brief.what_it_claims: When US stocks are down at least 5% from their peak and the project's fragility flag is also firing, Gold's price moves over the next one to four weeks spread out more in both directions. The claim is that this happens by more than Gold's own recent volatility would explain. It makes no claim about which way Gold goes.
brief.what_would_change_it: The entry would need to state plainly that the original 1.4 prediction failed at the one- and two-week horizons, and that the 1.2 bar was set after seeing the data. It would then treat the width prediction as observed rather than pre-registered and record the failure in its ledger. If the mechanism clause (the volatility-adjusted comparison, which was not changed) is kept as the sole pre-registered test, the entry could be resubmitted honestly. Showing the effect is not carried by 2010–2011 alone would also strengthen it.

findings.claim: The entry overstates the 20-day result. It quotes the Elevated cell's 20-day width as 7.67 and the ratio as 1.75. The report gives 6.67, which makes the ratio 1.52. The entry also contradicts itself on this point.

The same entry later says "The split shrinks once vol is divided out, from 1.31–1.52 to 1.18–1.29", which uses 1.52. §9 Q3: the entry "states what was measured ... and does not round it up." The pre-registered prediction (≥1.2 and not shrinking) still holds at 1.31/1.39/1.52. But the ledger that travels with the promoted read, and that the owner reads before deciding on a veto, inflates the largest effect by about a sixth. It must be corrected.

brief.case_against: First, the entry misreports its own evidence. At the 20-day horizon it says the gold-price spread in fragile periods was 1.75 times the normal spread. The report says about 1.5 times. The pre-set test still passed, but the record you would veto on overstates the biggest effect. That alone means it goes back for correction. Second, the evidence is narrower than it looks. The fragile, stressed days come from roughly four market episodes, and nearly two-thirds of them fall in 2010–2011. Third, the entry never checks whether 'fragile' is just another way of saying 'the stock market fell further'. Last, the entry states plainly that its chance of clearing the skill bar is low: on the practice data its score was about a fifth of the minimum required. Spending the one-time sealed read on it will very likely produce a negative Knowledge Base entry. That is legitimate, but it is a cost.
brief.what_it_claims: When the US stock market is already down at least 5% and the market-fragility alarm is on, gold's moves over the next one to four weeks spread out more in both directions than on equally stressed days without the alarm. They spread out more than gold's own recent volatility would explain, and the alarm says nothing about whether gold rises or falls. On the practice years before 2018 this held at all three horizons, and the test was written down before the data was looked at.
brief.what_would_change_it: Correct the 20-day numbers to match the report. The entry would then carry no blocking defect. It would be stronger still with three additions: an account of whether earlier runs of the same tool had already shown gold's spread in these cells; a check that the effect survives when deeper stock drawdowns (beyond 10%) are separated out; and a floor stated in distinct market episodes, not just runs below −5%. If the effect held with depth controlled, my concern about a hidden rival would be shown wrong.

brief.case_against:
The test was supposed to be a first look at data nobody had seen, the years from 2018 on. The practice run that produced the encouraging numbers used data through mid-2019. About a year and a half of that locked data has therefore already been looked at, and the good result partly rests on it. That is the one thing the rules forbid on the practice side.

With those locked years removed, the key group of days, when stocks are stressed and the fragility alarm is on, drops from 169 days to about 116. That is below the minimum of 150 days the entry set for itself. Roughly two-thirds of those days fall in 2010–2011, a period when Gold itself was unusually wild. What looks like a pattern may largely be one historical episode.

The entry's prediction was written honestly before the run and never moved, and every number it quotes matches the report. The problem is where the run looked, not how it was reported.
brief.what_it_claims: When US stocks are already down meaningfully and the project's fragility alarm is also on, Gold's price over the next one to four weeks becomes more spread out in both directions. It is not more likely to go up or down, only more uncertain. The entry also claims this extra spread is larger than Gold's own recent jumpiness would predict.
brief.what_would_change_it: Rerun the practice look on data ending 31 December 2017 only, and record that run and its end date in the ledger. Then check whether the stressed-and-alarm group still meets the 150-day and 8-episode minimum, and whether the spread ratios still clear their thresholds. The owner should also decide whether the 2018–2019 stretch that was already seen must be dropped from the final test. It would also help to show that the effect is not just deeper stock drops, by splitting at the −10% drop level, and that it does not come from 2010–2011 alone.

findings.claim: The confirm read is scored as a direction, not a width. The bar is the share of stressed, OR-Elevated days on which Gold's 20-day forward change is positive, which must exceed 55% against a coin-flip 50%. That is a sign with a confidence attached (§7, ADR-0009). The entry's target-space check describes a different test. The bar also contradicts the entry's own mechanism, which says the flag should not predict direction. So a pass of the bar would count against the mechanism, and an 'edge' verdict would require the mechanism to hold and fail at once.
findings.evidence: §2 'What would test it': "the confirm read: on stressed, OR-Elevated days, the share of days on which Gold's 20-day forward change is positive, against a coin-flip 50%. A share above 55% on the sealed slice, with a binomial interval clear of 50%, is the bar". §2 'Target-space check': "A width, and a two-sided one ... read by the distribution scorer. No location claim. Passes." §2 'Mechanism it would imply': "The flag should say nothing about which way Gold goes." The bar is unchanged since the first commit (§3, fc69b2c 2026-09-25), so this is a design defect, not a goalpost move.

findings.claim: The entry never says which hypothesis class it belongs to, and it does not adopt an existing class bar. If it is a shadow conditioner, WP-23.B's bar applies. That bar needs MIN_SKILL 0.02, a block-bootstrap interval clear of zero, the disqualifiers first and har_scaled as a second comparator, and the entry's confirm bar applies none of these. If it is a structure claim, §9 q7 requires its own class bar written before promotion, and none exists in WP-23.B. The ledger quotes 'the class bar's MIN_SKILL = 0.02' only as context for a low prior, not as the bar the read will face.
findings.evidence: §6 WP-23.B lists two classes: "Shadow conditioner vs `unconditional` (H-004, H-008)" and "Gap → width (H-003)". H-101 is in neither. §2 ledger: "all far under the class bar's `MIN_SKILL = 0.02`. That is the honest prior for the sealed read". §2 'What would test it' sets a binomial 55% share as "the bar".

findings.claim: The explore result clears the 11-spell floor on paper but is concentrated in time. About two thirds of the Elevated cell's days fall in 2010–2011, and the 11 spells come from roughly three macro stress periods (2010–11, 2014, 2015–16). The spell count is also a count of runs of the S&P below −5%, which can split one crisis into several runs. The raw width result is therefore closer to three episodes than eleven. This does not change what a sealed read would mean, but it should temper the prior.

brief.case_against: The entry's idea is about spread: when US stocks are stressed and the fragility flag is on, Gold's outcomes should fan out in both directions, without saying which way. The test it would actually spend the one sealed read on asks something else: does Gold go up on more than 55% of those days? That is a bet on direction. The project's rules forbid tests of that kind, because direction calls have already failed here several times. The test even contradicts the entry's own story: if the idea is right, Gold should not lean either way, so the test should fail. The read would be spent answering the wrong question. The entry also never names which pre-agreed standard it is judged against, so there is no bar that was fixed for its type before it was chosen. Finally, the encouraging preliminary result leans mostly on the 2010–2011 period and about three stress episodes in total.
brief.what_it_claims: When the S&P 500 is at least 5% below its peak and the project's fragility alarm is on, Gold's next one-to-four-week moves spread out more in both directions than on stressed days without the alarm. It claims this spread is larger than Gold's own recent volatility would explain. On the pre-2018 data the spread was about a third to a half wider, and still about a fifth wider after allowing for Gold's volatility.
brief.what_would_change_it: Replace the direction test with a spread test that uses the project's existing distribution scorer. For example: on the sealed data, the alarm-on spread must beat both the no-condition baseline and the volatility-forecast rival by the agreed skill margin, with the volatility-adjusted width ratio kept as the mechanism check. Also name which class standard applies, or write a new one before promotion. The pre-registered prediction and the floors could stay as written, since they were fixed before the data was looked at and I found no number that disagrees with its report.

brief.case_against: The practice run that makes this idea look promising rests on two market episodes, not the many its size suggests. Of the 169 fragile-and-stressed days, 145 come from one stretch in 2011 and 24 from one in 2015. The entry's own rule says a sealed cell with fewer than eight separate episodes is too thin to judge, yet it reports only that the day count cleared its minimum. It says nothing of the episode count, which fails badly. 2011 was also the year Gold made a violent peak and crash for its own reasons, which could explain the wider spread without the proposed mechanism. The expected payoff is also small: the entry itself says the score it must beat is barely moved even if the effect is real. Spending the one irreversible sealed read on a pattern seen essentially once is poor value. The way the report counts episodes also looks inconsistent, which weakens the protection that minimum is meant to give.
brief.what_it_claims: When US stocks are already down meaningfully and the project's fragility alarm is also on, Gold's short-term outcomes spread wider in both directions than on stressed days without the alarm. They spread wider than Gold's own recent volatility would predict. The claim is about how wide the spread is, not which way Gold moves.
brief.what_would_change_it: The entry should state plainly that its practice evidence covers only two episodes, mostly one, and so is below its own minimum. It should also fix or explain how episodes are counted, so the sealed minimum of eight means eight genuinely separate episodes. Evidence that the pattern holds outside 2011, on earlier data or a counted additional look, would answer the main concern. It should also record whether the sealed period has already been read for a similar question.

brief.case_against: The entry says the harness was run once, in its standard configuration, and that the numbers it reports come from that one run. The project's own record says otherwise. The harness was also run the evening before, with a different definition of 'stressed' (a 3% drop instead of 5%) and a looser minimum cell size. That run is not on the entry's list of looks, and nothing says what it showed. The rules require every look to be written down, precisely so that trying a few settings and keeping the one that looks good cannot happen quietly. The entry's prediction was written before either run and did not change, so this is not proof of cherry-picking. It is, however, a false statement in the record that travels with the promotion. Separately, the supporting evidence is thinner than it looks. About two-thirds of the stressed-and-fragile days come from 2010–2011, and one of the two key ratios clears its bar only barely. The fragility flag is also partly built from Gold prices, which the entry does not mention. All-dates skill is tiny, so the one-time sealed read has a low chance of clearing the bar.
brief.what_it_claims: When US stocks are already down meaningfully and the project's fragility alarm is on, Gold's range of outcomes over the next one to four weeks is wider in both directions than on stressed days without the alarm. It is wider by more than Gold's own recent volatility would predict. The entry makes no claim about which way Gold moves.
brief.what_would_change_it: Add the 2025-09-25 run to the entry's list of looks, with its settings and what it showed, and correct the 'one run' wording. With that fixed, nothing I found blocks promotion. Beyond the fix, the entry would be stronger if it did three things. First, report how Gold-dependent the fragility flag is, or show the result with the Gold input removed. Second, give a sense of uncertainty on the width ratios. Third, report the explore-period comparison against the volatility-forecast rival, which the promotion bar also requires it to beat.
